passage.title: Rising Star: An Interview with Leo Vance
passage.text:
At just sixteen, Leo Vance has already made a name for himself in the world of competitive swimming. We caught up with him at his local training centre in Manchester. 'I started swimming when I was five,' Leo explains, drying off after a two-hour morning session. 'My parents took me to the pool every weekend, but I didn't really take it seriously until I joined a club at ten.'

Leo’s routine is demanding. He wakes up at 4:30 a.m. to be in the water by 5:15 a.m. 'It’s tough, especially in winter when it's dark and cold outside,' he admits. 'But when you’re in the pool, you forget the time. You just focus on your strokes.' Despite the hard work, Leo insists he has a normal social life. 'People think athletes don't have time for friends, but I make sure I see my mates on Friday nights. It’s important to switch off.'

His biggest challenge so far was the National Youth Championships last year. 'I was so nervous before the final race,' he recalls. 'I almost pulled out, but my coach reminded me why I started. I ended up winning silver.' That medal changed his perspective. 'It wasn't just about the prize; it was about proving to myself that I could handle the pressure.'

Looking ahead, Leo has his sights set on the international stage. 'The dream is the Olympics, obviously. But for now, I’m focused on improving my technique. My coach says I’m strong, but my turns need work.' When asked if he has any advice for other young athletes, he is humble. 'Don't let the sport define who you are. Enjoy it, work hard, but remember to have fun. If you stop enjoying it, you’ll never reach your potential.'

b) After he won his first medal.

d) He believes it is important to take breaks from training to see friends.

b) It meant he could stop training so hard.
c) It qualified him for the Olympic Games.
d) It made his parents very proud of him.

questions.question: What is Leo’s main piece of advice for young athletes?
options: a) Always listen to what your coach says.
b) Focus entirely on your sport to succeed.
c) Keep enjoying the sport to reach your goals.
d) Try to win as many medals as possible.

passage.title: A Weekend at the Local Food Market
passage.text: Last Saturday, I decided to visit the new food market in the town square. I had heard many people talking about the fresh produce and the friendly atmosphere. (1) __________ I arrived just as the stalls were opening, so it was still quite quiet. The smell of freshly baked bread and roasted coffee beans was everywhere. I walked slowly past the different stalls, looking at the colourful vegetables and local cheeses. (2) __________ I eventually stopped at a small stall that sold homemade honey. The owner was very kind and let me taste three different types before I made my choice. After buying a jar of honey, I felt hungry and looked for something to eat. (3) __________ It was filled with fresh herbs and local vegetables. It was probably the best lunch I have had in a long time. While I was eating, a local band started playing some relaxing music near the fountain. (4) __________ Many families were sitting on the grass, enjoying the sunshine and the music. It was a perfect way to spend a Saturday morning. I will definitely return next weekend to try some of the other delicious treats. (5) __________ It is a great addition to our town and I hope it stays for a long time.

passage.title: A Family Trip to the Mountains
passage.text: Last summer, my family and I decided to spend a week in the mountains. We had never been there before, so we were all very excited. We packed our bags and left early on Saturday morning. The drive was long, but the scenery was beautiful. When we arrived, we checked into a small wooden cabin. It was perfect (1) _____ us. The next day, we went hiking. My father wanted to climb the highest peak, but my mother preferred to stay near the lake. In the end, we made (2) _____ compromise and chose a path that went through the forest. It was quite challenging (3) _____ times, but we enjoyed every moment. During the trip, we saw many interesting animals, including a deer. We also took lots of photos (4) _____ show our friends back home. On our last night, we sat outside and looked at the stars. It was (5) _____ most peaceful experience I have ever had. We all agreed (6) _____ we would definitely like to return next year.

passage.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who recently opened her own restaurant at just twenty-two. Sarah, was it always your dream to be a chef? Sarah: Actually, no. I wanted to be a musician, but I loved cooking for friends. Then, I took a summer job in a kitchen and realised I preferred the heat of the stove to the stage! Interviewer: Was it difficult to start your own business so young? Sarah: The hardest part wasn't the cooking, but the paperwork. I spent weeks talking to banks and finding the right location. I almost gave up once, but my mentor encouraged me to keep going. Interviewer: What is the most popular dish on your menu? Sarah: Definitely the spicy vegetable stew. I thought people would find it too hot, but they love it. I use a secret spice mix from my grandmother. Interviewer: What do you do when you are not working? Sarah: I try to get away from food entirely! I go hiking or read books. If I stay in the kitchen too long, I lose my creativity. Interviewer: What advice would you give to other young people? Sarah: Don't be afraid to make mistakes. Every burnt meal is a lesson.

passage.title: A New Beginning
passage.text:
Moving to a new city is often described as an exciting adventure, but for me, it felt more like a challenge I wasn't ready for. Last summer, my parents announced that we were moving from our quiet village to the bustling city of Manchester. I had lived in the same house for fourteen years, and the thought of leaving my friends and my favourite local park was devastating.

When we first arrived, the noise was the biggest shock. Unlike the peaceful nights I was used to, the city never seemed to sleep. There were sirens, traffic, and people talking at all hours. For the first two weeks, I barely left my room. I felt like an outsider looking in, convinced that I would never fit into this fast-paced environment. I spent most of my time messaging my old friends, feeling sorry for myself.

However, everything changed when I joined a local photography club. I had always enjoyed taking pictures, and I thought it might be a good way to get out of the house. On my first day, I met a girl named Sarah who was also new to the area. We started exploring the city together, looking for interesting buildings and street art to photograph. Through her eyes, I began to see the city differently. Instead of just seeing traffic and noise, I started to notice the beautiful architecture and the vibrant culture.

It has been six months now, and I can honestly say I don't regret the move. While I still miss my old friends, I have built a new life here. I have learned that moving isn't just about changing your address; it is about changing your perspective. You have to be willing to step outside your comfort zone to find the hidden gems in any new place. If you are facing a big move, my advice is to find a hobby or a group that shares your interests. It makes the world feel a lot smaller and much friendlier.

passage.text: Last Saturday, I decided to visit the new food market in the town square. I had heard so many great things about the fresh produce and the friendly atmosphere. (3) __________ There were so many delicious options, from spicy street food to sweet pastries. I finally chose a small stall that sold traditional vegetable pies. If you are interested in swimming, our main pool is 25 metres long and has a special area for children. For those who prefer fitness, the gym is equipped with the latest machines, and we offer a variety of classes including yoga and aerobics. We are currently looking for a receptionist to join our team, so please check our website if you are interested. Membership fees are very reasonable, and if you sign up before the end of the month, you will receive a discount of 15 percent on your first year. We also have a cafe on the ground floor where you can relax after your workout. We look forward to seeing you there!

passage.text: Interviewer: Sarah, you've been blogging for five years now. What made you start? Sarah: I was working in an office and felt bored. I took a trip to Peru and realised I wanted to share my experiences. Interviewer: Was it hard to get started? Sarah: Yes, I didn't know anything about photography or writing for an audience. I had to learn everything from scratch. Interviewer: Many people think travel blogging is just a holiday. What do you say to them? Sarah: It's definitely not! I spend hours editing photos and researching locations. It's a full-time job. Interviewer: Do you ever get lonely? Sarah: Sometimes, but I meet so many interesting people on the road that it balances out. Interviewer: What is your favourite part of the job? Sarah: Seeing a place I've only read about in books. It's magical. Interviewer: Any advice for beginners? Sarah: Be yourself. Don't try to copy other bloggers. Authenticity is what people want to see.

passage.title: A Life-Changing Summer in Peru
passage.text: Last summer, I decided to do something completely different. Instead of spending my holidays at home, I signed up for a volunteer program in a small village in the Peruvian Andes. I had always wanted to travel, but I wanted to do more than just visit tourist sites; I wanted to make a real difference. When I arrived, I was surprised by how different everything was. The air was thin, the mountains were breathtaking, and the local community was incredibly welcoming. My main job was to help build a new classroom for the primary school. I had never held a hammer or painted a wall before, but the local builders were very patient with me. They taught me how to mix cement and how to work as part of a team. It was hard physical work, especially in the heat, but I felt a great sense of achievement every evening. In the afternoons, I helped the children with their English homework. They were so eager to learn, and we often spent hours laughing as we tried to communicate through gestures and simple words. Living without electricity and limited internet access was a challenge at first. I missed my friends and the comforts of home, but as the weeks passed, I realised that I didn't need those things to be happy. I learned to appreciate the simple things, like a shared meal or a beautiful sunset over the peaks. This experience changed my perspective on life. I realised that we don't need much to be happy, and that helping others is one of the most rewarding things you can do. I returned home with a new sense of purpose and a promise to myself that I would continue volunteering in the future. I have already started looking for local opportunities in my own city.

passage.text:
Modern cities are undergoing a significant transformation as urban planners prioritize the creation of green spaces. For many years, concrete and glass dominated the skyline, but now the focus is shifting towards parks and gardens. (1) ________. These areas act as the lungs of the city, filtering pollutants and providing a necessary escape from the noise of traffic.

Consequently, city councils are investing millions into converting unused industrial land into public parks. Some of these projects are quite ambitious, involving the planting of thousands of native trees and the creation of artificial lakes. (3) ________. 

However, maintaining these spaces requires careful planning and constant funding. It is not enough to simply plant grass and trees; the city must ensure that these areas remain safe and accessible for everyone. (4) ________. This includes installing proper lighting and creating well-maintained paths for walkers and cyclists. 

Ultimately, the goal is to create a sustainable urban environment where people and nature can coexist. (5) ________. By making cities greener, we are not only improving our quality of life today but also ensuring a healthier future for the next generation.

passage.text: Interviewer: Today we are talking to Sarah Jenkins, who designs video games for a living. Sarah, was it always your dream to work in this industry? Sarah: Actually, no. I studied architecture at university. I loved drawing buildings, but I found the work a bit slow. One day, a friend showed me how to code a simple game, and I was hooked. I realised that game design is like architecture, but you can build entire worlds that people can interact with. Interviewer: That sounds fascinating. What is the most challenging part of your job? Sarah: People think it is just playing games all day, but it is actually very stressful. We have strict deadlines. If the game isn't ready for the holiday season, the company loses a lot of money. Sometimes I spend 12 hours a day staring at code. Interviewer: Do you ever get tired of it? Sarah: Sometimes, but then I see someone playing a game I helped create, and their face lights up. That feeling is worth all the hard work. Interviewer: What advice would you give to young people wanting to enter the field? Sarah: Don't just play games—learn how they are made. Start with simple tools and don't be afraid to make mistakes. Your first game will probably be terrible, and that is perfectly fine!

passage.title: An Interview with Maya Lin
passage.text:
We talked to sixteen-year-old runner Maya Lin about her life on and off the track. Maya recently won the national junior 800-metre championship, but she remains surprisingly down-to-earth.

Interviewer: Maya, congratulations on your gold medal! How did you first get into running?
Maya: Thanks! Actually, it was by accident. When I was eleven, my school's running team was short of one person for a relay race. The coach saw me running to catch the school bus and asked me to fill in. I didn't even have proper running shoes! I ended up running really fast, and the coach suggested I join the club. Before that, I preferred playing video games and reading. I never imagined I would become an athlete.

Interviewer: How do you manage to balance your training with your schoolwork?
Maya: It isn't easy. I train for about two hours every day after school, and more on weekends. I have to be very organised. I do my homework on the bus or during lunch breaks. My friends are very understanding, though they sometimes complain that I can't hang out with them on Friday nights because I have to sleep early for Saturday morning practice. But they always come to support me at my races, which means a lot.

Interviewer: Do you ever feel too much pressure before a big race?
Maya: Definitely. Before a race, my hands shake and I feel sick. But my coach taught me to view that nervous energy as a positive thing. She says it shows my body is preparing to run fast. Once the race starts, all the worry disappears and I just focus on my breathing and my steps. I don't think about winning; I just try to beat my own personal best time.

Interviewer: What are your goals for the future?
Maya: Of course, the Olympics is the ultimate dream, but that is a long way off. For now, I want to focus on my next race and keep improving. I also want to finish my school exams with good grades because education is important to me. If I have one piece of advice for other young people, it's to try new things. You might discover a talent you never knew you had!

passage.text:
Woman: Did you see the photos I posted from my weekend walk?
Man: Yes, they're amazing! The lighting in the forest was perfect. I didn't know you were so good at photography.
Woman: Thanks! I've been practicing a lot, but I still struggle with getting the focus right on moving objects, like birds.
Man: Well, you've definitely got a talent for landscapes.

Woman: Do you want to see the new science-fiction film tonight?
Man: I've heard the special effects are incredible, but the story is quite weak and predictable.
Woman: Really? The reviews I read said the acting was brilliant, especially the main character.
Man: Well, I suppose we should judge for ourselves. Let's get tickets.

Man: How was your first Italian cooking class yesterday?
Woman: It was great! The chef was really funny and explained everything clearly.
Man: Did you make pasta from scratch?
Woman: Yes, though mine turned out a bit too thick. Still, it tasted amazing, and I learned some useful techniques that I can easily try at home.

Girl: Are you coming on the mountain hike this weekend?
Boy: I'd love to, but my boots are completely worn out. I need to buy a new pair before I do any serious climbing.
Girl: You could always borrow my brother's. He's got some spares.
Boy: Thanks, but hiking boots need to fit perfectly, otherwise you get terrible blisters. I'll just go shopping on Saturday instead.

Boy: Did you see the photos I took at the park yesterday?
Girl: Yes, they're really good! The lighting on the lake was perfect. But why didn't you get closer to the birds? They look a bit small.
Boy: I know, but I didn't want to scare them away. Next time I'll use a better zoom lens.
Girl: Good idea. Still, you've got a real talent for finding great angles.

Man: I'm thinking of giving up the guitar. I've been practicing for three months and I still can't play a whole song.
Woman: Don't be so hard on yourself! It takes time. Are you practicing every day?
Man: Well, only on weekends, really. I'm too tired after work.
Woman: That's the problem. Even fifteen minutes a day during the week would make a huge difference.

passage.text:
Hello everyone, and thank you for joining our tour group today. I want to give you some practical information about our visit to the Science Museum tomorrow.

First, we will meet outside the main entrance at 8.45 am. Please don't be late as the bus leaves at exactly nine o'clock.

When we arrive, we will start our visit in the transport gallery on the ground floor. This is always very popular because of the old steam trains.

After that, you will have some free time. I highly recommend visiting the special exhibition on the first floor. It is about robots and how they are used in everyday life.

For lunch, you can eat your own sandwiches in the picnic area, which is next to the museum shop. Please do not eat inside the exhibition rooms.

In the afternoon, we have booked a special 3D film in the IMAX cinema. The film is about the history of space exploration. It starts at two-thirty and lasts for forty minutes.

Finally, before we go home, you can visit the gift shop. If you show your group ticket, you can get a discount on books and posters.

Are there any questions?

passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Elena Rossi, a successful travel blogger. Elena, welcome. Why did you first start your blog, 'Elena's Footsteps'?

Elena: Well, I didn't plan to make it my job! I actually started it when I went on a gap year to South America. My parents were really worried, so I promised to write regular updates so they'd know I was safe. I didn't think anyone else would read it, but then other travellers started finding my posts and asking for advice.

Interviewer: That's amazing. You've been to so many countries. Which one stands out the most?

Elena: People always ask this! I love Japan for its food, and Iceland for the landscapes, but my absolute favourite was Albania. I didn't know much about it before going, but the local people were incredibly welcoming. One family even invited me into their home for dinner when I got lost. That kindness is what I remember most.

Interviewer: Travelling isn't always easy, though. How do you deal with things when they go wrong?

Elena: Oh, I've had missed flights, lost luggage, and food poisoning! At first, I used to get really stressed and angry. But I quickly realised that doesn't help. Now, I just accept that problems are part of the adventure. I try to stay calm and look for a solution, often by asking locals. They are usually happy to help a confused tourist.

Interviewer: You usually travel by yourself. Do you prefer that?

Elena: I do. When you travel with friends, you tend to stay in your own little bubble. But when you're on your own, you're forced to talk to strangers, which means you make new friends much faster. Of course, it can be lonely occasionally, but the freedom to decide where to go next without arguing is worth it.

Interviewer: What's the most challenging part of being a professional blogger?

Elena: People think it's a permanent holiday, but it's hard work. The toughest thing for me is the lack of a routine. I'm constantly moving, which makes it hard to exercise regularly or eat healthily. I don't mind the long hours spent editing photos or writing posts, because I love doing that, but not having a proper home base can be exhausting.

Interviewer: Finally, what tips do you have for someone wanting to start a travel blog?

Elena: Don't just write about the famous tourist spots that everyone knows. Try to find a unique angle. Write about your personal feelings and the small details, like the smell of a local market. And most importantly, write because you love it, not because you want to get free hotel rooms. Readers can tell if you aren't being genuine.

Interviewer: Thank you, Elena!

passage.title: My summer with the sea turtles
passage.text:
When I finished school last year, most of my friends went straight to university. I wasn't sure what I wanted to study, so I decided to spend three months as a volunteer on a sea turtle project on a small Greek island. My parents weren't very keen at first. They thought I should get a job and save money instead, but when I showed them that the organisation had been running for over twenty years, they began to feel more relaxed about it.

I arrived in June, just as the turtles were starting to lay their eggs on the beaches. There were about fifteen volunteers from all over the world, and we lived together at a simple campsite with tents and a shared kitchen. I'd never been camping before, and I'll be honest: the first week was hard. It was extremely hot, there were insects everywhere and I missed having my own room. But I soon got used to it, and by the end I actually preferred sleeping outside.

Our main job was to walk along the beaches early in the morning, looking for the tracks the turtles had left in the sand during the night. When we found a nest, we protected it with a metal cage so that dogs and foxes couldn't dig up the eggs. We also put up signs asking tourists not to use umbrellas or chairs near the nests. Most visitors were very interested and asked lots of questions, although a few were annoyed that part of the beach was closed.

What surprised me most was how much time we spent talking to people. Every evening, two volunteers ran an information stand in the harbour. I was terrified the first time because my Greek was limited to 'hello' and 'thank you', and many of the visitors were Greek families. However, the other volunteers helped me, and I learnt enough phrases to explain the basics. By August I was confident enough to give short talks to groups of children, which is something I would never have imagined doing a year earlier.

The best moment came near the end of my stay, when the first eggs hatched. Watching dozens of tiny turtles run across the sand towards the sea at midnight is something I will never forget. Only about one in a thousand will survive to become an adult, which made me realise why the project's work matters so much.

Looking back, I think the experience taught me more than any classroom could. I've now decided to study marine biology, and I'm hoping to return to the island next summer as a team leader. If you're thinking of volunteering, my advice is simple: don't choose a project just because it looks good in photos. Find out exactly what the work involves, and make sure it's something you really care about.

passage.title: The rise of online learning
passage.text:
Twenty years ago, learning a new language or studying for a qualification usually meant sitting in a classroom at a fixed time each week. Today, millions of people learn at their kitchen table, on the bus or even in bed. (1) ______ In some countries, more than half of all adults have now taken at least one course on the internet.

There are several reasons for this growth. The most obvious is that the internet has become faster and cheaper, so watching video lessons is no longer a problem for most people. (2) ______ For example, a nurse who works nights can study during the day, while a parent can wait until the children are asleep.

Universities have also played a part. Many of them now put recordings of their lectures on the internet. (3) ______ Some of these have attracted over a million students, which would be impossible in any lecture hall.

However, online learning is not perfect. Many people sign up for a course with great enthusiasm but never finish it. (4) ______ Without a teacher checking their progress, they find it easy to put off the next lesson until tomorrow, and then the day after.

To solve this problem, many course designers now include ways for learners to stay in touch with each other. (5) ______ Students who feel part of a group, it seems, are much more likely to reach the end. In the future, the best courses may combine the freedom of learning online with the support that classrooms have always provided.

passage.text:
Girl: Hi Sam, it's Maya. It's about tomorrow. I know I said we'd meet at the ticket office, but it's always really crowded there in the morning. I thought about the café, but I've just remembered it's closed on Sundays. So let's meet under the big clock by the main entrance instead. It's easy to find. See you there at nine!

Woman: Hi Tom, it's me. I'm still at the station, and I'm afraid I'm going to be late. My train to York was supposed to leave at ten fifteen, but there's a problem with the signals. At first they said it would leave half an hour late, so at quarter to eleven. But they've just changed it again on the board, and now it says eleven o'clock. So I'll probably get to you around lunchtime. Sorry!

Driver: Good morning, everyone, and welcome aboard this coach to Edinburgh. The journey normally takes three hours, and that includes a short stop at a service station. But I'm afraid there are roadworks near Newcastle today, so we expect to arrive about half an hour later than usual. That means the whole trip will take around three and a half hours. Don't worry, though. Last winter, in the snow, it took us over four hours!

Woman: So, did you pack everything for your trip?
Man: I thought so. I checked my passport about three times, and I remembered to put my phone charger in at the last minute. But guess what? I left my sunglasses on the kitchen table! And it's supposed to be sunny all week.
Woman: Oh dear. Well, you can always buy some at the airport.
Man: I suppose so, but they're so expensive there.

Woman: A single to Cambridge, please.
Man: That's twelve pounds. Are you coming back today? Because an off-peak day return is only fourteen.
Woman: Oh, yes, I'm coming back this evening.
Man: Then the return is much better value. We also sell a weekly pass, but that's only worth it if you're travelling every day.
Woman: No, it's just today. I'll take the return, then.

Man: So how are you getting to the airport on Friday?
Woman: Well, I was going to take the bus because it's the cheapest, but it takes nearly two hours with all the stops. My brother offered to drive me, but his car's at the garage until next week. So in the end I've booked a seat on the train. It's only forty minutes, and the station is right next to the terminal.
Man: Sounds perfect.

Man: Excuse me, is this where the Oxford train goes from? Platform seven?
Woman: Well, it normally leaves from platform seven, but not today. They're doing some building work over there, so it's going from platform three instead.
Man: Three? Do I need to go over the bridge?
Woman: No, it's just past platform five, on this side. You can't miss it.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

passage.text:
Coach: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for staying behind after training. I've got some exciting news about the club. As you know, we've been raising money for something new for over a year. A lot of you were hoping for a swimming pool, but I'm afraid that was far too expensive. Instead, we've built an indoor climbing wall, and it's ready to use from next week.

Now, if you've never climbed before, don't worry. We're running beginners' classes. We originally planned to have them on Tuesday evenings, but the hall is already busy then, so they'll be on Thursday evenings from seven till eight thirty.

What do you need? Well, you don't need to buy special shoes, because the club will lend you a pair, and we'll give you a helmet as well. But please bring your own water bottle. Climbing is hard work, and we can't sell drinks in the hall.

There's also a special offer. Last year new members got a free T-shirt, but this year anyone who joins before the end of May will get a free sports bag with the club logo on it.

To book a place on a class, you'll need to go to reception. We're hoping to add bookings to the website soon, but it isn't working properly yet, so please don't try that for now.

Finally, we need volunteers for July. The summer barbecue is already organised, thanks to the parents' committee, but we still need people to help with the fun run through the park. If you're free, please put your name on the list by the door. Thanks, everyone!

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 4.
passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Helen Price, who works as a ranger in a national park in the north of England. Helen, why did you choose this job?
Helen: People often assume I wanted to escape the city, but actually I loved living in London. And the money certainly isn't the reason anyone becomes a ranger! No, it really goes back to when I was about ten. A ranger took our school group out at night to look for badgers, and I remember thinking, that's what I want to do when I grow up.
Interviewer: What's the hardest part of the job?
Helen: Everyone expects me to say the weather, but I've got good clothes, and I actually enjoy a stormy day. The hours can be long in summer, but I don't mind that either. What I find really difficult is when visitors leave rubbish or let their dogs chase the sheep, even though there are signs everywhere. I'm not comfortable telling people off, but sometimes I have to.
Interviewer: The park has had far more visitors in recent years. How do you feel about that?
Helen: Some of my colleagues worry about the paths getting damaged, but we've repaired most of them now, so I'm not too concerned. And the car parks get busy at weekends, but it's never really crowded up on the hills. Honestly, I'm delighted. So many people have discovered the outdoors, and that can only be a good thing.
Interviewer: Has technology changed your work?
Helen: A lot. We use cameras to count the animals, and there's an app for reporting problems like fallen trees. They save us loads of time, and they don't cost as much as people think. But a camera can't tell you why the deer have moved to a different valley. You still need someone who really knows the land.
Interviewer: What would you say to young people who'd like to do your job?
Helen: A degree can help, but it isn't essential. Some of the best rangers I know never went to university. Some people start by working in visitor centres, which is fine, but you don't learn much about the land there. The best thing is to volunteer. Parks are always looking for helpers, and it's the only way to find out if you really love the work.
Interviewer: And what about your own future?
Helen: I was offered a job training new rangers at our head office, but I turned it down. I'd be sitting at a desk all day. I did once think about working in a national park in Canada, but I'd miss this place too much. No, I'm happy right where I am, and I hope I'll still be here when I retire.

passage.title: Singing in the square
passage.text:
Every Saturday morning, Leah Morgan, 26, takes her guitar and a small speaker to the square outside Bristol's main shopping centre. For the next four hours she sings to anyone who stops to listen. We asked her about life as a street musician.

How did you start?
'Almost by accident. I'd been playing in cafés for a couple of years, but they only paid me in free coffee! One day a friend dared me to play outside the railway station. I was terrified – my hands were shaking so much that I could hardly play the right notes. But a little girl stood in front of me and danced through every song, and by the end I'd completely forgotten my nerves. I went home with more money than I'd ever earned in a café.'

Is it hard work?
'People think we just turn up and play, but there's a lot more to it. In Bristol you need a permit from the city council, and there are rules about how loud you can be and how long you can stay in one place. I also check the weather forecast all the time. Rain is bad, obviously, but a very hot day is almost as bad, because people hurry from shop to shop and don't want to stand still.'

What's the best thing about it?
'The audience is completely honest. In a concert hall, people have paid for a ticket, so they stay even if they're bored. On the street, if you're not good enough, they simply walk away. That can be hard, but it has made me a much better performer. I've learnt to notice straight away when I'm losing people, and to change the song.'

Does anyone ever complain?
'Occasionally. A man who works in one of the shops used to come out and ask me to turn the music down. At first I was annoyed, but then I realised he had to listen to me all day. Now I play my quieter songs when I'm near his door, and he sometimes brings me a cup of tea!'

What are your plans?
'A few people have offered to manage me, and I've recorded some songs, which I sell as downloads. But I'm in no hurry to give up the street. I don't think I'd ever get the same feeling in a studio. Even if I become famous one day – which I doubt – I'd like to come back to the square now and then, just to remind myself where it all began.'

passage.title: How I learnt Portuguese
passage.text:
Learning a new language as an adult can feel impossible. Three years ago I moved to Lisbon for work without knowing a single word of Portuguese. Today I can chat comfortably with my neighbours and even argue with the plumber. Here is what worked for me.

First, I stopped trying to study for hours at the weekend. (1) ______ Instead, I spent twenty minutes on Portuguese every single day, usually on the bus to work. Short, regular practice turned out to be far more effective than long, tiring sessions.

Second, I learnt the words I actually needed. Textbooks often begin with colours and animals, but I needed to buy bread, pay bills and ask for directions. (2) ______ That list became my first vocabulary book, and because I was using the words every day, I remembered them easily.

My third tip is to accept that you will make mistakes. For months I was so worried about saying something wrong that I hardly spoke at all. (3) ______ She told me that people would be pleased I was trying, and she was right. Most people I met were patient and helpful, and some even corrected me in a friendly way.

It also helps to bring the language into your free time. I changed the language on my phone to Portuguese and started watching films with Portuguese subtitles. (4) ______ After a while, though, I found I could follow a whole film without stopping it once.

Finally, find a reason to speak that has nothing to do with lessons. I joined a local running club, where nobody spoke English. (5) ______ Now some of those runners are my closest friends, and I no longer think about which language I'm speaking.

Learning a language takes time, and there is no magic method. But if you practise a little every day and don't give up, you will be surprised how far you can go.

passage.text:
Twenty years ago, most people were nervous about buying things online. Today, millions of us (1) ______ our weekly shopping without leaving the house. But how do we decide what to buy?

passage.title: From a village to the city
passage.text:
Last year I left my small village in Wales and moved to Manchester to start my first job. I had never lived anywhere bigger (1) ______ our local market town, so I was quite nervous.

At first, everything felt strange. I was afraid (2) ______ getting lost, so I carried a map everywhere, and at night the noise of the traffic kept me awake. I didn't know anyone in the city, and neither (3) ______ my flatmate, who had just arrived from Spain. We spent most evenings watching television in our tiny kitchen.

Things got better when I found (4) ______ about a climbing club near my office. We went along together one evening, and now we go twice a week. Most of our friends here are people we met on the climbing wall.

These days I really enjoy city life. (5) ______ is always something to do, from free concerts in the park to street markets at the weekend. Rents are expensive, and I sometimes miss the quiet countryside. At (6) ______ same time, I can't imagine going back now. Moving to Manchester was one of the best decisions of my life.

passage.text:
Man: Would you like something to drink with your meal?
Woman: Yes, a fresh orange juice, please.
Man: I'm really sorry, but our juice machine isn't working today. We've only got apple juice in bottles.
Woman: Oh, I don't really like apple juice. I'll have a cup of tea, then. Actually, no, I'm so tired this morning. Could I have a coffee instead? A large one, please.
Man: Of course. Milk and sugar?
Woman: Just milk, thanks.

Man: Right, that's two large margherita pizzas. They're nine pounds each, so that comes to eighteen pounds.
Woman: Oh, isn't there a special offer on Tuesdays? The poster in the window says two pounds off.
Man: That's right, if you collect the order yourself.
Woman: Great. So that's sixteen pounds, then?
Man: Actually, it's two pounds off each pizza, not the whole order. So you only pay fourteen.
Woman: Even better! Here you are.
Man: Thanks. Enjoy your meal.

Mum: Hi, love. Did you manage to get everything on the list?
Girl: I think so. Here's the milk, and I got the big box of eggs, like you said.
Mum: Lovely, thanks. And the butter? I need it for the birthday cake this afternoon.
Girl: Oh no, I knew there was something. I was looking at the list on my phone and the battery died.
Mum: Never mind. Could you pop back to the shop for it? It's only five minutes away.
Girl: OK, I'll go now.

Man: Excuse me, are we too late for breakfast?
Woman: No, you're fine. From Monday to Friday we stop serving breakfast at eleven, but at weekends we carry on until half past eleven. And today's Saturday, so you've still got about twenty minutes.
Man: Oh, that's lucky.
Woman: Then we start the lunch menu at twelve o'clock, if you'd prefer something bigger.
Man: No, breakfast is perfect, thanks. Two full English, please.

Man: Shall we try that new Italian restaurant on the high street tonight?
Woman: I rang them this morning, actually. They're fully booked until Saturday.
Man: Oh, what a shame. Well, we could just cook something here instead.
Woman: There's nothing in the fridge, though, and I really don't want to go shopping now. What about the burger bar near the station? It's cheap, and you don't need to book.
Man: Good idea. I haven't been there for ages. Let's go at about seven.

Woman: That was delicious. What would you recommend for dessert?
Man: Well, the chocolate cake is the most popular, but to be honest it's quite heavy after a big meal like yours.
Woman: Mm, I am quite full. What about the fruit salad?
Man: It's fine, but it's nothing special. If I were you, I'd have the apple pie. Our chef makes it fresh every morning, and it comes with ice cream.
Woman: That sounds lovely. I'll try that, then.

Woman: Hi there, what can I get you?
Man: I was going to have the chicken salad, but it says on the board that it's finished.
Woman: Sorry, yes, we sold the last one about ten minutes ago. The soup of the day is still available, though. It's tomato, and it comes with fresh bread.
Man: Hmm, I had tomato soup at home last night, so I don't really fancy it again. I'll just have a cheese sandwich, please.
Woman: No problem. Brown or white bread?
Man: Brown, please.

passage.text:
Woman: Are you taking that jacket back to the shop? I thought you loved it.
Man: I do. The colour's great, and it fits me perfectly.
Woman: So what's the problem? Did you decide it was too expensive?
Man: No, it was actually in the sale, so it was a real bargain. But look at this. The zip's broken already, and I've only worn it twice.
Woman: Oh, that's annoying. Have you still got the receipt?
Man: Yes, luckily. I'm hoping they'll just give me a new one.

Man: Have you been to the new shopping centre yet?
Woman: Yes, I went on Saturday. Everyone told me it would be really crowded, but actually it was fine. I didn't have to queue anywhere.
Man: And what are the shops like?
Woman: Well, that's the thing. They're the same big chain stores you find in every town. I was hoping for some smaller, independent places, you know, something a bit different. So it was a bit disappointing, really.
Man: What about parking? That's always a nightmare in town.
Woman: Oh, that was great. It's free for the first three hours, and there were loads of spaces.

Woman: Did you see the post office has changed its opening hours? It's open until seven on weekdays now.
Man: Yes, I saw the notice.
Woman: Were you surprised?
Man: Not really. People had been asking for longer hours for ages. But it makes such a difference to me. I could never get there before five because of work, so I had to send all my parcels on Saturdays, and the queue was always awful.
Woman: I thought you'd be annoyed, because it's closed on Saturday afternoons now.
Man: That doesn't matter to me any more. I can just go on my way home.

Man: I really need a haircut, but I hated what the last place did to me.
Woman: You should try Sam's on Bridge Street. I've been going there for years.
Man: Is it cheap?
Woman: Not especially. It's about the same as everywhere else. And you have to book at least a week ahead, because it's always busy.
Man: So why do you like it so much?
Woman: Because they actually listen to you. They ask exactly what you want before they start cutting, and you come out looking the way you asked. That's rare, believe me.

Woman: The Sunday market was much bigger than I expected, wasn't it?
Man: Yes, there were loads of stalls. The clothes were a bit disappointing, though. It was mostly cheap T-shirts.
Woman: Really? I didn't think so. I found a lovely wool scarf for five pounds. But the food stalls were amazing.
Man: Absolutely. They were the best thing there. That Thai curry I had was fantastic.
Woman: I know. I'd go back just for the food, to be honest.

Girl: Dad, could you give me a lift into town on Saturday morning?
Dad: What for? Is it for that new phone? You know it's cheaper if you buy it online.
Girl: I know, and I'm not going to buy it in the shop. I'll order it online when I get home. I just want to see it properly first, and hold it in my hand. It looks quite big in the photos, and I want to check it'll fit in my pocket.
Dad: That's sensible. OK, I'll drive you in after breakfast.

Presenter: And now some news for everyone who's planning to go to the Millbrook Summer Festival next weekend. As many of you know, for the last five years the festival has been held in the town square. This year, though, it's moving to Castle Park, because the organisers needed more space for all the new events.

The main stage won't be in the same place as before, either. Last year it was right next to the car park, and lots of people complained about the noise from the traffic. This time you'll find it next to the lake, which should be a lovely setting for the evening concerts.

There's plenty for younger visitors, too. Sadly, the painting competition won't be happening this year, but instead there's a cake decorating competition on Saturday afternoon for anyone under twelve. The winner gets a family ticket for next year's festival.

Now, a practical tip. There will only be a small number of chairs, and they're mainly for older visitors. So the organisers suggest that you bring a blanket to sit on. And please don't bring umbrellas, because they block the view for people behind you.

Tickets cost twelve pounds at the entrance, but if you buy them online before Thursday, you'll only pay eight pounds. Children under five get in free.

Finally, getting there. There's very little parking near Castle Park, and taxis will be expensive that weekend. So the best thing to do is to take the shuttle bus from the railway station. It runs every twenty minutes and it's free if you show your festival ticket.

So, that's everything for now. Have a great time at the festival!

passage.text:
Interviewer: Today I'm talking to Lucy Grant, who has just been chosen for the national swimming team at the age of seventeen. Lucy, when did you first start swimming?
Lucy: I was seven. Everyone assumes I loved it from the very beginning, but actually I was terrified of putting my face in the water. My older brother was the keen one. I only went along because Mum didn't want to drive to the pool twice. The lessons themselves were fun, though. Our teacher turned everything into a game.

Interviewer: Now you train at five o'clock in the morning. That must be hard.
Lucy: People always say that's the worst part. And at first I hated hearing the alarm. But now I actually love it. The pool's really quiet, and I feel I've already achieved something before the day starts. My teachers used to ask if I fell asleep in class, but I'm more awake than anyone! What I find harder is the evenings, when my friends go out and I have to be in bed by nine.

Interviewer: You changed coaches two years ago. Why was that?
Lucy: My first coach was lovely, and she had loads of experience. The club was just round the corner from my house, too. But she mainly worked with sprinters, and I'd started to realise that I was better at longer races, like the eight hundred metres. So I joined a club that specialises in distance swimming. It means a longer journey, but it was the right decision.

Interviewer: Last year you didn't make the final at the national championships. How did you deal with that?
Lucy: Of course I was disappointed for a day or two. Some people said I'd been unlucky, because I had a cold that week, but that wasn't really it. When my coach and I watched the video, it was obvious that my starts were too slow. So we worked on them all winter. Looking back, it was the best thing that could have happened, because I'm much faster now.

Interviewer: You're quite popular on social media. How do you feel about that side of things?
Lucy: Some swimmers say it adds a lot of pressure, but I don't feel that at all. And I only post once a week, so it doesn't take up much time. The best thing is when girls send me messages saying they've joined a swimming club because they watched my videos. That makes it all worth it.

Interviewer: Finally, what advice would you give to young swimmers?
Lucy: Don't worry about finding the perfect club or buying expensive kit. And please don't compare yourself with other swimmers all the time. The most important thing is to make sure you're having fun. If you aren't enjoying it, you won't keep going when it gets difficult.
Interviewer: Lucy Grant, thank you very much.

passage.title: Waiting for the perfect picture
passage.text:
Wildlife photographer Emma Hartley talks about her work.

People often imagine that my job involves travelling to beautiful places and taking amazing pictures every day. The truth is rather different. I spend most of my time waiting – sometimes for days – and on many trips I come home without a single photo I'm happy with.

I became interested in wildlife when I was about ten. My grandfather lent me his old camera, and I used to sit in his garden trying to photograph the birds at the feeder. Most of the pictures were terrible, but I loved the challenge of staying still and quiet for so long. I didn't think of photography as a career, though. At university I studied biology, and I planned to become a scientist.

Everything changed during my final year, when I joined a research trip to Scotland to count sea birds. I took my camera along just for fun, but one of the scientists saw my photos and sent them to a nature magazine. To my surprise, they printed three of them. That was when I realised that I could combine my two interests.

The first few years weren't easy. I earned very little and had to work in a camera shop at weekends to pay the rent. But the job taught me a lot about equipment, and I met photographers who gave me useful advice.

Nowadays I work mainly for magazines and conservation organisations. Before a trip, I spend weeks reading about the animal I want to photograph: where it feeds, when it is most active and how it reacts to people. Good preparation matters far more than an expensive camera. Last spring, for example, I wanted to photograph otters in Norway. Local fishermen told me the otters came out at dawn, so I was in my hiding place by four o'clock every morning. On the sixth day, a mother and two young otters appeared just metres away.

The part of the job I find hardest is not the cold or the early mornings but being away from my family. My son is seven now, and I try not to accept jobs that last more than two weeks.

Young people often ask me how to start. My answer is always the same: begin close to home. You don't need to travel to Africa. A local park is full of wildlife if you are patient enough to look for it. And remember that the animal always comes first. If it seems stressed, put your camera down and walk away. No photo is worth frightening an animal.

passage.title: Why teenagers need their sleep
passage.text:
Most parents have had the same experience. They knock on their teenager's bedroom door at nine o'clock on a Saturday morning. There is no answer. It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy. (1) ______

During the teenage years, the body's internal 'clock' changes. This clock controls our daily pattern of sleeping and waking. The brain starts producing melatonin, the chemical that makes us feel sleepy, around two hours later than it did in childhood. (2) ______ But school still starts at the same time, so the alarm goes off long before their bodies are ready to wake up.

Sleep matters at every age, but it is especially important for teenagers. Experts say teenagers need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. Surveys show that most of them get fewer than seven. (3) ______ Students who sleep too little find it harder to concentrate in class and to remember what they have learnt. They are also more likely to feel anxious or low. They catch colds more often, too. Their results in sport can suffer as well.

Phones make the problem worse. Many teenagers take them to bed and message friends or watch videos until late. (4) ______ The light from the screen also tells the brain that it is still daytime, so melatonin arrives even later.

So what can teenagers do? There are some simple answers. Sleep experts suggest going to bed at the same time every night, even at weekends, and leaving phones in another room. (5) ______ Some schools in the UK and the USA have even started lessons an hour later, and teachers there say that students are more awake and get better marks. Perhaps other schools will soon follow their example.

passage.text:

passage.title: Listen and answer the questions in Part 1.
passage.text:
Man: Excuse me, I'm here for the Year 10 parents' evening. Is it in the library, like last term?
Woman: Not this time, I'm afraid. The library's being painted this week. We'd planned to use the dining room, but it's too small for all the teachers' tables, so everyone's in the main hall. Just go down this corridor and it's the double doors on your left.
Man: Great, thanks very much.

Girl: Dad, Mrs Palmer says everyone in the orchestra has to take something to the concert tomorrow evening.
Man: Not your music stand again? It's still in the car from last time.
Girl: No, the school's got plenty of those now. And they've borrowed chairs from the church hall, so we don't need to bring our own. It's the lights, actually. The hall will be quite dark while we're playing, so we all need a small torch to read our music.
Man: I think there's one in the kitchen drawer. I'll check the batteries.

Girl: Are you going to be in the talent show, Josh? I thought you might play your guitar.
Boy: I did think about it, but loads of people are doing music. And I'm definitely not dancing. You've seen me try!
Girl: So what are you going to do, then?
Boy: I've been writing some funny stories about school life. I'm going to stand up on stage and tell jokes. Mr Grant says it's fine as long as I'm kind about the teachers.
Girl: That'll be brilliant.

Girl: Guess what, Gran? I came first in the school art competition!
Woman: Oh, well done, love! What did you get? Last year the winner got a big box of paints, didn't they?
Girl: They did, but I've already got loads of paints. This year the winner got a ticket for the new exhibition at the city gallery, and I can take someone with me. The girl who came second got a book of famous paintings.
Woman: That sounds lovely. So who are you taking?
Girl: You, of course!

Boy: Did you hear about the Year 9 trip? We were supposed to be going to the castle, but Mr Hughes says the coach company can't do that date.
Girl: So is it cancelled?
Boy: No, they've changed it. We're going to the science museum in the city instead, because the train goes straight there. Some people wanted the farm park, but that's closed until the spring.
Girl: Oh well, the museum's got that new space exhibition, so I don't mind.

Woman: Hello, this is a message for all parents from Kingsmead School. Sports day is going ahead this Friday, but please note that the start time has changed. The races were going to begin at half past ten, but because very hot weather is forecast for the afternoon, the first races will now start at quarter past nine. Students should arrive at school at nine o'clock as usual, wearing their PE kit, and bring a bottle of water. Thank you.

Woman: You're not playing computer games already, are you? What about your homework?
Boy: I've done the maths worksheet. I finished it at lunchtime. And the science poster isn't due until next Friday.
Woman: So there's nothing else?
Boy: Well, there's the history essay. Mr Dean wants it on his desk first thing tomorrow morning, and I've only written the introduction.
Woman: Then the games can wait, can't they?

passage.text:
Woman: So you've started your engineering course. What's it like?
Man: It's hard work. The lectures are long, but the lecturers make them really interesting. What I love most, though, is the time in the workshop. Last week we built a small bridge and tested how much weight it could take. That's why I chose engineering, really.
Woman: And it's four years, isn't it? That seems a long time.
Man: It goes quickly when you enjoy it.

Girl: I heard you're giving up your job at the café. Is it the money?
Boy: No, the pay's actually quite good for a weekend job, and Sue, the manager, is lovely. It's just that my exams start in May, and at the moment I'm working every Saturday and Sunday. I've got so much revision to do that something has to go.
Girl: Will they let you come back in the summer?
Boy: Sue says they will, so that's good.

Man: So, what do you think of the new office, now we've been here a week?
Woman: I was worried it'd be really noisy with everyone in one big room, but actually it's been fine. And because the design team sit right next to us now, I can just turn round and ask them things instead of sending emails. We've sorted out more problems this week than in the whole of last month.
Man: The journey's worse for me, though. It's a much longer walk from the station.
Woman: Oh, it's about the same for me.

Woman: Have you got a minute, Mr Clarke?
Man: Of course, Helen. If it's about your holiday dates, I've already said yes.
Woman: Thanks, but it's not that. I heard that Tom's team is behind with the new website. I've finished all my own work for this month, so I wondered if I could join them for a couple of weeks.
Man: That would be a big help, actually. Tom will be delighted.

Boy: How was the interview for the summer job at the museum?
Girl: They kept me waiting for twenty minutes, which wasn't ideal, but I didn't really mind because it gave me time to calm down. And then it went better than I expected. I'd read all about the museum beforehand, so I could answer all their questions, and they even laughed at my joke about the dinosaurs!
Boy: It sounds like you'll get it.
Girl: Well, I really think I've got a good chance.

Woman: How's your online Spanish course going?
Man: Well, I'm not sure about the teacher. She talks really fast and she doesn't always explain the grammar.
Woman: I've found that with mine too. But for thirty pounds a term, you can't really complain, can you? The evening class at the college costs four times that.
Man: That's true. You get a lot for the price. And the lessons are only forty minutes, which suits me.
Woman: Me too. I couldn't concentrate for any longer after work.

passage.text:
Woman: Good morning, everyone. I'm Kate Morris, the manager of the new Riverside Sports Centre, and I'd like to tell you what we're offering when we open next month. The opening day is Saturday the twelfth of March. We were hoping to open in February, but the builders needed a little more time to finish everything.

The centre has a twenty-five-metre swimming pool, a sports hall and a gym. But the thing we're proudest of is our climbing wall, which is the tallest in the region. Beginners are very welcome. You don't need any experience, because an instructor will be with you all the time.

Membership costs thirty-two pounds a month for adults, and students and people over sixty-five pay twenty pounds. And if you join before the opening day, your first month is completely free.

We've also got something special on Sunday mornings. The pool will be open only for parents and children, and there'll be games and floating toys in the water.

Lots of people have asked us about getting here. There is a car park, but it only has forty spaces, so we'd really recommend coming by bike. We've put a large bike shelter right next to the main entrance. The number fourteen bus stops outside too, but it only runs once an hour.

Finally, if you'd like to look around before you join, we're running free tours every afternoon this week. They leave from the reception desk at four o'clock, and they take about half an hour. I hope to see lots of you there.

passage.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Leila Ahmed, who designs video games. Leila, how did you first get interested in making games?
Leila: People often think I had a teacher who pushed me, but actually my teachers thought games were a complete waste of time. And I certainly didn't expect to get rich! What happened was that as a teenager I used to change the levels in the games I'd bought. I'd add new rooms, make the monsters harder, that kind of thing. I enjoyed that far more than just playing them.
Interviewer: And then you went to university?
Leila: Yes, I studied games design. The programming was hard, and at one point I thought about switching to an art course, but I'm glad I didn't. Looking back, the most useful thing was the group projects. In this industry nobody works alone, and that's where I learnt to listen to other people's ideas and share my own.
Interviewer: What was your first job like?
Leila: It was at a small company in Manchester. I'd imagined I'd spend my days inventing characters, but in fact I spent most of my time playing the same level again and again to find mistakes. I had no idea how much testing goes into a game. It wasn't boring exactly, it taught me to be patient, and my boss was very kind to me. I just hadn't expected it.
Interviewer: What do you think makes a really good game?
Leila: Well, everyone talks about the graphics, and of course a good story helps. But for me, if a player can't understand what to do in the first two minutes, they'll stop playing, however beautiful the game looks. So simple rules come first. Everything else is built on that.
Interviewer: Some parents worry that young people spend too much time on games. What's your view?
Leila: I don't think games are bad for young people at all. Lots of them teach you to solve problems. But I've got two children myself, and they have to go outside and see their friends as well. An hour or so after their homework seems about right to me. And I don't mind whether it's an educational game or not. To be honest, a lot of educational games aren't very good!
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to listeners who'd like to design games?
Leila: Don't wait. You don't have to go to university first, and you certainly don't need to start as a tester like I did. There are free programs that let you build a small game in a weekend. Make something simple, show it to your friends and listen carefully to what they say. That's how you learn.
Interviewer: Leila Ahmed, thank you very much.

Interviewer: What was your first job like?
Leila: It was at a small company in Manchester. I'd imagined I'd spend my days inventing characters, but in fact I spent most of my time playing the same level again and again to find mistakes. I had no idea how much testing goes into a game. It wasn't boring exactly, it taught me to be patient, and my boss was very kind to me. I just hadn't expected it.
Interviewer: What do you think makes a really good game?
Leila: Well, everyone talks about the graphics, and of course a good story helps. But for me, if a player can't understand what to do in the first two minutes, they'll stop playing, however beautiful the game looks. So simple rules come first. Everything else is built on that.
Interviewer: Some parents worry that young people spend too much time on games. What's your view?
Leila: I don't think games are bad for young people at all. Lots of them teach you to solve problems. But I've got two children myself, and they have to go outside and see their friends as well. An hour or so after their homework seems about right to me. And I don't mind whether it's an educational game or not. To be honest, a lot of educational games aren't very good!
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to listeners who'd like to design games?
Leila: Don't wait. You don't have to go to university first, and you certainly don't need to start as a tester like I did. There are free programs that let you build a small game in a weekend. Make something simple, show it to your friends and listen carefully to what they say. That's how you learn.
Interviewer: Leila Ahmed, thank you very much.

passage.title: The teenager who helped a whole street
passage.text:
When sixteen-year-old Maya Collins started building an app in her bedroom two years ago, she had no idea that it would soon be used by more than fifty thousand people. 'Honestly, I just wanted to solve a problem in my own family,' she says.

The problem began one winter. Maya's grandmother slipped on some ice and broke her leg. She lived alone, and although Maya's parents visited as often as they could, they both worked long hours in another town. 'Gran's neighbours kept telling us they would happily help her with shopping or collecting medicine,' Maya explains. 'But they never knew when she actually needed something, and she was too proud to knock on their doors and ask.'

That gave Maya the idea for Next Door, an app which lets older people post small requests that neighbours nearby can accept with one click. There was only one difficulty: Maya had never written a line of computer code. She spent the next six months teaching herself from free online videos, often working until midnight at weekends. 'My first version was a disaster,' she laughs. 'It crashed every time more than two people used it at once.'

Help came from an unexpected place. Maya's computer science teacher, Mr Okafor, noticed her working on the app during a lunch break and offered to look at it with her. 'He didn't fix it for me,' she says. 'He just asked the right questions until I understood what I'd done wrong. That was much more useful.'

After a few more months of testing with her grandmother's neighbours, Maya put Next Door online. At first only a handful of families in her street joined, but then a local radio station interviewed her, and the number of users grew almost overnight. Today the app is used in towns all over the country.

Several companies have since offered to buy Next Door, but Maya has turned them all down. 'They wanted to add advertising and charge people to use it,' she says. 'The people who need it most are often the ones with the least money, so that's not going to happen.'

Maya admits it hasn't always been easy to balance the app with her schoolwork, especially during exams. She now spends only Sunday afternoons on it, and a small team of volunteers answers users' messages during the week.

Her advice for other young people with an idea is simple. 'Don't wait until you feel ready, because you never will. Start with something small, and expect it to go wrong. That's how you learn.'

passage.text:
Woman: If we drive to Edinburgh, we can stop wherever we like on the way.
Man: True, but it's eight hours at the wheel, and parking in the city centre is a nightmare.
Woman: Mm, fair point. And on the train we could read or sleep.
Man: Exactly. And it's not much more expensive if we book now.
Woman: Right, let's do that. But I'm not getting up at five to catch the first one!
Man: No, the one at ten is fine. What about the hotel?
Woman: I'd still prefer somewhere outside the centre. It's quieter.
Man: Hmm. We can sort that out later.

Man: So how was the camping trip? You weren't very keen before you went.
Woman: I know! I thought I'd hate sleeping in a tent, and when it rained on the first night I nearly came home. But honestly, it turned out to be one of the best holidays I've ever had. The campsite was lovely, it cost almost nothing, and I didn't miss my phone at all.
Man: So you'd go again?
Woman: Definitely.

Man: Good morning, Skyway Airlines. Is this about the delays on today's flights?
Woman: No, no, my flight isn't until next week. I'm booked to Rome on the fourteenth, reference AB172. My sister's wedding has been moved, so I won't need to be there until the sixteenth. Could you put me on a flight that day instead? I'm happy to pay the difference. Oh, and I've already read the information about hand luggage, so I don't need to ask about that.
Man: Let me see what I can do.

Man: You're off to Spain again? Visiting your cousins?
Woman: Not this time. They're coming over here in the summer. I've booked a two-week course in Seville. My Spanish is getting really rusty, and I'll need it for my new job.
Man: Lucky you. Seville's near the coast, isn't it?
Woman: Not that near, and anyway I doubt I'll have time for the beach. There are classes every morning and homework every evening!

Woman: How was the hotel in Lisbon?
Man: The rooms were a bit small, and I'd read online that the street outside was noisy, but actually we didn't hear a thing at night. What I really liked was that it was right in the old town, so we could walk everywhere. The breakfast was great too, lots of fresh fruit and local cakes.
Woman: Sounds perfect.

Woman: I'm thinking of doing a weekend in Paris. Have you ever done a city break?
Man: A couple. They're not as expensive as people think, if you book early. And I don't mind all the walking, actually. My problem is that by the time you've found your way around, it's time to go home. I'd rather go somewhere for a whole week and really get to know the place.

passage.text:
Mrs Hughes: Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Mrs Hughes, and I'm going to give you the main details of next term's school trip to Barcelona. We'll be away for five days, from the second to the sixth of April. We'll be flying from Manchester, not Liverpool as I said in my first letter, so please remember that.

In Barcelona we'll be staying in a youth hostel near the beach. Students will share rooms of four, and each room has its own bathroom. Breakfast and dinner are included, but you'll have to buy your own lunch, so bring some extra money for that.

On the first full day we'll visit the famous church, the Sagrada Família, and in the afternoon there's a guided walk around the old part of the city. On the Thursday we're going to spend the morning at a local secondary school, where you'll have lessons with Spanish students of your own age. Several of you asked about the football stadium. Unfortunately, it's closed for building work while we're there, so instead we'll go to the science museum, which I promise is great fun.

The total cost of the trip is three hundred and ninety pounds. You need to pay a deposit of eighty pounds by the end of this month, and the rest before the fifteenth of February.

As for what to pack, the weather in April can be quite changeable, so bring a waterproof jacket as well as sun cream. And please don't forget your passport. Every year somebody leaves it at home! Mobile phones are allowed, but you must hand them in to a teacher at ten o'clock each night.

If you have any questions, please email me rather than phoning the school office. Thank you.

passage.text:
Interviewer: My guest today is Hannah Price, who at just twenty-four is head chef at her own restaurant. Hannah, how did it all start?
Hannah: I was sixteen and I got a Saturday job washing up in a hotel kitchen. I'd always loved cooking at home, so I thought I knew what to expect, but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet… I honestly wasn't sure I'd last. Funnily enough, I didn't mind the washing-up itself. It was nice just to be able to watch the chefs.
Interviewer: And then you went to catering college.
Hannah: That's right. People assume college taught me to cook, but honestly I learnt most of my skills in real kitchens. The written work was easy for me, actually, because I've always liked reading about food. What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business. One of them introduced me to the chef who gave me my first proper job.
Interviewer: Lots of young people get interested in cooking through TV competitions. What do you think of them?
Hannah: My mum loves them, and she's always telling me to apply for one, but I'd never do it, and I don't really watch them myself. My problem is that they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes. Real restaurant work is mostly cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night.
Interviewer: Two years ago you opened your own restaurant. Why?
Hannah: Everyone thinks it's about the money, but I earn less now than when I worked for someone else! And my last boss was brilliant. I still ring him for advice. The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up. It's the kind of food nobody in the city was serving.
Interviewer: What's it like being such a young head chef?
Hannah: Inside my kitchen, it's fine. My team know what I can do. But suppliers sometimes ask to speak to 'the chef' when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me. I don't think being young makes me better or worse at cooking, and I've spent eight years in kitchens, so experience isn't really the issue.
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who want to become chefs?
Hannah: Don't sign up for a course straight away. Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first, even if it's just washing up, and see if you can cope with it. Plenty of people discover it isn't for them, and that's fine. And don't try to learn every kind of food. Getting a few dishes really right is worth much more.

Interviewer: My guest today is Hannah Price, who at just twenty-four is head chef at her own restaurant. Hannah, how did it all start?
Hannah: I was sixteen and I got a Saturday job washing up in a hotel kitchen. I'd always loved cooking at home, so I thought I knew what to expect, but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet… I honestly wasn't sure I'd last. Funnily enough, I didn't mind the washing-up itself. It was nice just to be able to watch the chefs.
Interviewer: And then you went to catering college.
Hannah: That's right. People assume college taught me to cook, but honestly I learnt most of my skills in real kitchens. The written work was easy for me, actually, because I've always liked reading about food. What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business. One of them introduced me to the chef who gave me my first proper job.
Interviewer: Lots of young people get interested in cooking through TV competitions. What do you think of them?
Hannah: My mum loves them, and she's always telling me to apply for one, but I'd never do it, and I don't really watch them myself. My problem is that they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes. Real restaurant work is mostly cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night.
Interviewer: Two years ago you opened your own restaurant. Why?
Hannah: Everyone thinks it's about the money, but I earn less now than when I worked for someone else! And my last boss was brilliant. I still ring him for advice. The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up. It's the kind of food nobody in the city was serving.
Interviewer: What's it like being such a young head chef?
Hannah: Inside my kitchen, it's fine. My team know what I can do. But suppliers sometimes ask to speak to 'the chef' when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me. I don't think being young makes me better or worse at cooking, and I've spent eight years in kitchens, so experience isn't really the issue.
Interviewer: Finally, what would you say to young people who want to become chefs?
Hannah: Don't sign up for a course straight away. Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first, even if it's just washing up, and see if you can cope with it. Plenty of people discover it isn't for them, and that's fine. And don't try to learn every kind of food. Getting a few dishes really right is worth much more.

questions.question: How did Hannah feel when she first worked in a kitchen?
questions.explanation: She thought she knew what to expect, 'but I was shocked. The heat, the noise, twelve hours on your feet'. She 'wasn't sure I'd last', so she was not sure about the job, and she says she 'didn't mind the washing-up itself', so she was not bored.
options: a) Surprised by how hard the work was
b) Bored by the simple tasks she had to do
c) Sure that she had chosen the right job

questions.question: What does Hannah say was most useful about catering college?
questions.explanation: She says 'What really mattered was that my tutors knew everyone in the business', and one of them introduced her to the chef who gave her her first job. She learnt most of her skills 'in real kitchens', not at college, and the written work was already easy for her.
options: a) She learnt most of her cooking skills there.
b) It helped her with the written work.
c) She met people who helped her find work.

questions.question: What is Hannah's opinion of cooking competitions on TV?
questions.explanation: She says 'they make it look as if being a chef is all about exciting moments and big prizes', while real work is 'cooking the same dishes perfectly, night after night'. She says 'I'd never do it', and it is her mum who loves them; she doesn't really watch them herself.
options: a) She would like to take part in one, as her mum suggests.
b) They are fun to watch with her family.
c) They give the wrong idea of what chefs do.

questions.question: Why did Hannah open her own restaurant?
questions.explanation: 'The real reason was that I wanted to cook with ingredients from the farms around here, where I grew up.' She earns less now than before, and she says her last boss 'was brilliant'.
options: a) She wanted to use food from her local area.
b) She hoped to earn more money than before.
c) She did not get on with her last boss very well.

questions.question: How does Hannah feel about being a young head chef?
questions.explanation: Suppliers 'ask to speak to the chef when I'm standing right in front of them, and that still annoys me'. She says being young doesn't make her 'better or worse at cooking', and with eight years in kitchens 'experience isn't really the issue'.
options: a) Worried that she does not have enough experience.
b) Annoyed that some people don't see her as the chef.
c) Sure that her age makes her a better cook.

questions.question: What advice does Hannah give to young people who want to be chefs?
questions.explanation: She says 'Get a part-time job in a real kitchen first … and see if you can cope with it'. She tells them not to sign up for a course straight away, and not to try to learn every kind of food.
options: a) Go to catering college as soon as possible.
b) Get some experience in a real kitchen first.
c) Learn to cook as many kinds of food as possible.

You must answer this question. Write your answer in about 100 words.

Read this email from your English-speaking friend, Alex, and the notes you have made.

From: Alex
Subject: Guess what!

Hi!

I've got some great news: I've found a flat to rent, and it's in your neighbourhood! I'm moving in at the end of next month. (Note 1: Great!)

I don't know the area at all yet. What's the best thing about living there? (Note 2: Tell Alex)

I'll need to do a lot of shopping for the flat. Where do you think I should go? (Note 3: Suggest…)

And would you like to help me on moving day? I'll buy you lunch! (Note 4: Yes, but…)

See you soon,
Alex

Write your email to Alex using all the notes.
